subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which adaptation of the alveolar epithelium most directly reduces the diffusion distance for gases?
options: A large total surface area provided by millions of alveoli
Squamous (flattened) epithelial cells forming a wall one cell thick
Surfactant lining the alveolar surface
A rich capillary network surrounding each alveolus
questions.explain: Flattened squamous cells make the alveolar wall extremely thin, minimising the distance gases must diffuse.

questions.q: Antigenic variation makes some pathogens (e.g. influenza virus) hard to combat because:
options: They change their surface antigens, so memory cells from previous infections no longer recognise them
They cannot be engulfed by phagocytes
They reproduce too slowly for memory cells to form
They destroy all the host's T-cells
questions.explain: Frequent changes to surface antigens mean existing memory cells are no longer complementary, so a new primary response is needed each time.

questions.q: At high altitude, where the partial pressure of oxygen is low, the oxygen dissociation curve of a well-adapted animal is often shifted to the LEFT because:
options: Carbon dioxide levels are always higher at altitude
Tissues require less oxygen at altitude
Haemoglobin must release oxygen more readily to tissues
A higher oxygen affinity helps haemoglobin load oxygen at the low oxygen partial pressures found there
questions.explain: A leftward shift (higher affinity) allows haemoglobin to become saturated despite the low oxygen partial pressure of high-altitude air.

questions.q: The ELISA test uses antibodies linked to an enzyme to:
options: Detect the presence of a specific antigen or antibody by producing a colour change
Replace a missing hormone
Vaccinate a patient against a disease
Destroy a pathogen in a sample
questions.explain: In an ELISA, an enzyme-linked antibody binds its target and the enzyme then catalyses a colour change, revealing presence and amount.

questions.q: The basement membrane of the glomerulus prevents which component of blood from entering the filtrate?
options: Glucose
Plasma proteins such as albumin
Urea
Water
questions.explain: The basement membrane acts as a molecular sieve, holding back large plasma proteins and blood cells while small molecules pass through.

questions.q: Compared with elastic recoil in expiration, why are the walls of arteries elastic?
options: To enable exchange of materials with tissues
To slow blood flow for absorption
To allow active contraction that pumps blood
To stretch under high pressure and recoil, smoothing out pressure surges and maintaining flow
questions.explain: Elastic tissue in artery walls stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, evening out pulsatile pressure and sustaining blood flow.

questions.q: In the cell-mediated response, cytotoxic (killer) T-cells destroy infected body cells by:
options: Stimulating B-cells to divide
Secreting antibodies that agglutinate them
Releasing perforin, which makes holes in the cell membrane so the cell dies
Engulfing them by phagocytosis
questions.explain: Cytotoxic T-cells release perforin that perforates the membrane of infected cells, causing them to die before the pathogen can multiply.

questions.q: In the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction shortens the sarcomere because:
options: The actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten
Calcium ions are pumped out of the sarcoplasm
The H zone widens as filaments slide apart
Myosin heads form cross-bridges and pull the actin filaments past the myosin toward the centre
questions.explain: Myosin heads bind actin and, powered by ATP, pull the thin filaments inward so the sarcomere shortens while filament lengths stay the same.

questions.q: When the water potential of the blood falls, ADH is released and causes:
options: Less water to be reabsorbed, producing dilute urine
Increased filtration at the glomerulus
More aquaporins to be inserted into the collecting duct, increasing water reabsorption
The loop of Henle to pump out more sodium
questions.explain: ADH makes the collecting duct walls more permeable by inserting aquaporins, so more water is reabsorbed and concentrated urine is produced.

questions.q: Phosphocreatine is important in muscle contraction because it:
options: Rapidly regenerates ATP from ADP at the start of intense exercise
Provides the calcium needed for contraction
Forms the cross-bridges with actin
Binds to troponin
questions.explain: Phosphocreatine donates a phosphate to ADP to quickly resynthesise ATP, sustaining contraction during short bursts of activity.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections such as HIV?
options: Viruses are too large to be affected
Viruses lack the metabolic processes and structures (e.g. cell walls, ribosomes) that antibiotics target
Antibiotics only work on fungi
Viruses have thicker cell walls
questions.explain: Antibiotics target bacterial structures and processes; viruses use host-cell machinery and lack these targets, so antibiotics do not affect them.

questions.q: Activated T-helper cells assist the humoral response chiefly by:
options: Producing large amounts of antibody themselves
Directly killing pathogens with toxins
Releasing cytokines that stimulate B-cells and phagocytes
Engulfing antigen-presenting cells
questions.explain: T-helper cells secrete cytokines (interleukins) that promote clonal expansion of B-cells and increase phagocytic activity.

questions.q: At a synapse, transmission is unidirectional because:
options: The synaptic cleft is too wide for diffusion
Acetylcholinesterase is found only presynaptically
Calcium ions only enter the postsynaptic neurone
Neurotransmitter receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane and vesicles only on the presynaptic side
questions.explain: Vesicles releasing neurotransmitter are confined to the presynaptic neurone and receptors to the postsynaptic membrane, so signals pass one way.

questions.q: Why does positive feedback rarely operate in mammalian homeostasis?
options: It amplifies a deviation away from the normal level, which is usually harmful
It cannot involve hormones
It uses too little energy to be effective
It returns a factor to its set point too quickly
questions.explain: Positive feedback drives a factor further from normal, so it is unsuitable for stabilising the internal environment except in special cases like childbirth.

questions.q: Recovering from chickenpox and becoming immune to it is an example of:
options: Natural passive immunity
Natural active immunity
Artificial active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
questions.explain: The body makes its own antibodies and memory cells in response to a natural infection, giving natural active immunity.

questions.q: In a pregnancy test, monoclonal antibodies are used to:
options: Bind specifically to the hCG hormone, giving a coloured line when present
Destroy the hCG hormone
Convert hCG into a dye
Produce hCG in the urine
questions.explain: Mobile antibodies bind hCG and are then trapped by immobilised antibodies in the test window, producing a visible coloured line.

questions.q: In a control system, a receptor, a coordinator and an effector act in sequence. The coordinator's role is to:
options: Receive information from receptors and instruct effectors to respond
Detect the change in the environment
Set a new value for the factor being controlled
Bring about the corrective response
questions.explain: The coordinator (e.g. brain or endocrine gland) processes input from receptors and signals effectors to produce an appropriate response.

questions.q: A person's urine is tested and found to contain glucose. This most likely indicates that:
options: Their kidneys are filtering too little blood
The loop of Henle is too long
Blood glucose was so high that it exceeded the capacity of the co-transporters to reabsorb it all
ADH secretion has stopped
questions.explain: When blood glucose is very high (as in untreated diabetes), the reabsorption carriers become saturated, so glucose remains in the urine.

questions.q: For herd immunity to interrupt transmission of a pathogen, the proportion of the population that must be immune depends mainly on:
options: The age of the youngest individual
The colour of the vaccine vial
The cost of the vaccine
How easily the pathogen spreads from person to person
questions.explain: More infectious pathogens require a higher proportion of immune individuals to break chains of transmission and protect the susceptible.

questions.q: Ringing experiments, in which a ring of bark (and phloem) is removed from a tree trunk, support the role of phloem in translocation because:
options: The xylem also stops functioning
The leaves immediately wilt
Water stops reaching the leaves above the ring
Sugars accumulate in the bulge above the ring while tissues below may die
questions.explain: Sugars cannot pass the removed phloem, so they build up above the ring, showing phloem carries organic solutes.

questions.q: ADH is produced by the hypothalamus and released from the:
options: Kidney medulla
Pancreas
Adrenal cortex
Posterior pituitary gland
questions.explain: ADH is synthesised in the hypothalamus and stored in and released from the posterior pituitary gland.

questions.q: How is the magnitude (intensity) of a stimulus conveyed to the central nervous system?
options: By the size of each action potential
By the speed of the action potential
By the frequency of action potentials and the number of neurones firing
By the duration of the resting potential
questions.explain: Because action potentials are all-or-nothing, a stronger stimulus is signalled by a higher firing frequency and recruitment of more neurones.

questions.q: In the cell-mediated response, T-helper cells are activated when they:
options: Release antibodies into the plasma
Bind to antigens presented on the surface of an antigen-presenting cell
Bind directly to free antigens in the blood
Engulf the pathogen by phagocytosis
questions.explain: T-helper cells have receptors complementary to antigens displayed by antigen-presenting cells, and this binding activates them.

questions.q: A vaccine typically contains antigens that produce long-lasting immunity by:
options: Destroying the pathogen directly
Supplying ready-made antibodies
Stimulating the body to make memory cells without causing the disease
Providing passive protection only
questions.explain: Vaccines present harmless antigens that trigger a primary response and memory-cell formation, so future exposure is met rapidly.

questions.q: The cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have many mitochondria and microvilli because they:
options: Secrete ADH into the filtrate
Produce urine of variable concentration
Carry out a large amount of active reabsorption requiring ATP and surface area
Filter the blood under high pressure
questions.explain: Reabsorbing most of the glucose, ions and water demands abundant ATP (mitochondria) and a large absorbing surface (microvilli).

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes differs from type 2 in that:
options: Type 1 results from autoimmune destruction of beta cells so little or no insulin is produced
Type 1 is caused by target cells losing responsiveness to insulin
Type 1 is usually treated by diet and exercise alone
Type 1 has a later onset and is linked to obesity
questions.explain: In type 1 the immune system destroys insulin-secreting beta cells, whereas type 2 involves reduced insulin sensitivity of target cells.

questions.q: Glucose released into the blood by gluconeogenesis is produced from:
options: Glucose absorbed from the gut
Non-carbohydrate sources such as amino acids and glycerol
Glycogen stored in the liver
Fatty acids converted directly to glucose
questions.explain: Gluconeogenesis synthesises new glucose from non-carbohydrate molecules such as amino acids and glycerol, mainly in the liver.

questions.q: Antibodies passed from mother to baby in breast milk give the baby:
options: Artificial active immunity
Natural passive immunity
Natural active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
questions.explain: The antibodies are received naturally (via milk/placenta) and the baby does not make them itself, so it is natural passive immunity.

questions.q: In a healthy person, beta cells of the islets of Langerhans detect a rise in blood glucose when:
options: Glycogen is broken down in the liver
Glucagon binds to their surface receptors
Adrenaline is secreted by the adrenal glands
Glucose entering the cell increases ATP, closing potassium channels and triggering insulin release
questions.explain: Increased glucose uptake raises ATP, closing K+ channels; the resulting depolarisation opens Ca2+ channels and triggers insulin secretion by exocytosis.

questions.q: An antibody is a glycoprotein with a quaternary structure made up of:
options: A single polypeptide chain
One heavy and three light chains
Two heavy and two light polypeptide chains held by disulfide bonds
Four identical heavy chains
questions.explain: Each antibody consists of two identical heavy and two identical light chains linked by disulfide bridges, forming a Y-shaped molecule.
